title: The Gift Episode

jokes.text: Jason Alexander? Uh, only if we can't get Michael Richards or Jerry Seinfeld. So Jason Alexander. That's excellent.
jokes.setup: The booking team is running down guest options, presenting Jason Alexander as a viable get.
jokes.punchline: Artie reveals Alexander is the bottom of the Seinfeld cast hierarchy — a third choice who gets cheerfully confirmed as 'excellent' the moment he's the only option.
jokes.explanation: Sharp Hollywood insider comedy — the implicit rankings within a cast are an industry reality, and the immediate pivot to 'that's excellent' nails the late-night booking desperation. Economy is high; it lands in two lines.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Jason Alexander? Uh, only if we can't get Michael Richards or Jerry Seinfeld.

jokes.text: Mary Lou Retton? Marilu Henner. Oh, thank God. The last thing we need is Larry on those uneven bars again.
jokes.setup: Someone mishears 'Marilu Henner' as Olympic gymnast 'Mary Lou Retton.'
jokes.punchline: Artie's relief is explained by the absurd image of Larry Sanders attempting Olympic gymnastics — a joke that implies past disasters without spelling them out.
jokes.explanation: This is a genuinely excellent joke. It uses the malapropism as a springboard to a punchline that perfectly characterizes Larry (vain, reckless, physically unqualified) while being economical and specific. 'The last thing we need' implies a history of Larry's poor judgment. Character integration is high — this only works because we know Larry would absolutely try.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Mary Lou retton? Marilu henner. Oh, thank God. The last thing we need is Larry on those uneven bars again.

jokes.text: Danny DeVito, Jimmy Walker, the potato lady, and the Breeders. Uh, rock band.
jokes.setup: The lineup is read off: a movie star, a comedian, a novelty act, and 'the Breeders.'
jokes.punchline: The clarification 'uh, rock band' — delivered after a beat — implies someone in the room thought 'the Breeders' was a second potato-lady-style novelty act, or something even more disturbing.
jokes.explanation: The beat before the clarification does a lot of work — it signals confusion in the room and lets the audience feel superior. Economy is near-perfect. Doesn't reach higher because the joke relies entirely on the lineup juxtaposition rather than character.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Oh, my gosh! Good one, Artie. Oh, I liked their first album, but the second one was a disappointment.

jokes.text: They got the stain completely out... Tell Darlene I said hi. What'd you think of the lineup tonight?
jokes.setup: Larry is supposed to be focused on the booking meeting; he instead becomes fixated on a newly cleaned suit.
jokes.punchline: He sends personal regards to the dry cleaner's employee mid-meeting, then pivots back to work as if nothing happened — complete obliviousness to the absurdity.
jokes.explanation: A classic Larry move — self-absorption expressed through mundane obsession. Works because it's true to character and the pivot is seamless. Doesn't build to a strong punchline, more of a character texture beat.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: They got the stain completely out. I can't believe it. Well, we'll use them as our regular dry cleaner from now on.

jokes.text: Are we ordering lunch? No, Hank. We're not. Oh, because I heard someone mention potatoes, and I can have those on my new diet.
jokes.setup: Hank wanders into a booking meeting, confused about its purpose.
jokes.punchline: He heard 'potato lady' and thought it was a lunch order — and has already calculated whether potatoes fit his diet. Hank's self-involvement is total.
jokes.explanation: Pure Hank. His logic is airtight from inside his own head — he heard potatoes, assumed food, checked his diet. The joke works because Tambor's Hank is a character defined by his obliviousness masquerading as awareness. Character integration is very high.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Are we ordering lunch?

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: No, Hank. We're not.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh, because I heard someone mention potatoes, and I... I can have those on my new diet.

jokes.text: Why is Larry in here? Well, Larry likes to be involved in deciding who the guests will be.
jokes.setup: Hank challenges Larry's presence in his own booking meeting.
jokes.punchline: Paula's straight-faced explanation — that the host of the show likes input on guests — is played as if it's an eccentric quirk rather than a completely reasonable thing.
jokes.explanation: The comedy comes from Hank's complete self-centeredness — he can't conceive of why the host would be in the booking meeting. Functional character comedy, not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Please do, because I only have the one shake in the morning.

jokes.text: Hold on, Beverly. We're ordering lunch, I think. Is there a menu? We're not ordering.
jokes.setup: The meeting keeps getting derailed; now Beverly (or another staffer) is drawn in.
jokes.punchline: The cascade of confusion — Hank telling Beverly they ARE ordering despite just being told they're NOT — compounds the dysfunction comically.
jokes.explanation: Part of a sustained chaos escalation — each new element deepens the meeting-derailment comedy. Functional, not standout.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: His agent said he wouldn't be feeling well tonight.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Yeah, I've had that.

jokes.text: Please do, because I only have the one shake in the morning.
jokes.setup: Artie tells Hank he'll be kept 'advised' about the meeting — a polite dismissal.
jokes.punchline: Hank responds with a diet update that has no logical connection to being kept advised about booking — his stream of consciousness is entirely self-referential.
jokes.explanation: The non-sequitur diet update delivered as a perfectly logical response is quintessential Hank. The comedy is in his sincerity — he genuinely thinks his one morning shake is relevant information.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Well, perhaps the fact that we pay them scale and send 'em home with a piece of shit t-shirt and hat...

jokes.text: Why did Devito cancel? His agent said he wouldn't be feeling well tonight. Yeah, I've had that.
jokes.setup: Danny DeVito has canceled because his agent said he 'wouldn't be feeling well tonight.'
jokes.punchline: Larry responds 'Yeah, I've had that' — as if canceling in advance for a future illness is a relatable medical condition, not a transparent excuse.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's tightest jokes. 'Yeah, I've had that' is delivered as genuine empathy for a transparently fake excuse, which reveals Larry's own familiarity with the dodge. The economy is surgical — four words contain an entire worldview. Quotable, sharp, perfectly Larry.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I really appreciate the effort that you put into your job each day.

jokes.text: I can't be held responsible for certain personality types... It means there are certain performers with certain neuroses and mental shortcomings that make it completely impossible for me to deal with them on a normal level.
jokes.setup: Larry presses Paula on why guests keep canceling.
jokes.punchline: Paula's explanation for her booking failures is that the guests are mentally defective — delivered with complete self-righteousness, zero self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: Paula blaming the neuroses of Hollywood performers for her own failures is both satirically accurate (Hollywood is full of neuroses) and a perfect character beat. The escalating specificity — 'neuroses AND mental shortcomings' — adds punch.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Okay, what he said was: 'I really appreciate the effort you put into your job each day.'

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Ooh, girl, you are fucked.

jokes.text: ...perhaps the fact that we pay them scale and send 'em home with a piece of shit t-shirt and hat.
jokes.setup: Larry diplomatically says Paula shouldn't feel criticized and he appreciates her effort.
jokes.punchline: Paula ignores the diplomacy and blurts out that the real problem is the show's terrible gift policy — 'a piece of shit t-shirt and hat.'
jokes.explanation: Great structural beat — it punctures Larry's diplomatic overture AND plants the 'gift' theme that drives the episode. Economy is high. 'Piece of shit t-shirt and hat' is genuinely funny in its specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I don't think she's got the right personality. I think she's too... abrasive? No, it's, uh... brusque? No. Incapable of putting a performer at ease because she's has a basic contempt for the business.

jokes.text: Well, thank you. You're doing a great job. / What did Larry say to you that's got you so scared? / 'I really appreciate the effort you put into your job each day.' / Ooh, girl, you are fucked.
jokes.setup: Beverly asks what Larry said that has Paula so scared. Paula quotes Larry's suspiciously warm, HR-speak compliment verbatim.
jokes.punchline: Beverly's instant diagnosis — 'Ooh, girl, you are fucked' — confirms that corporate positive-speak is universally understood as a death sentence, funnier for being in the mouth of a supporting character.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is near-perfect: Larry's obsequious praise (played straight in scene) is recontextualized by Beverly's blunt translation. 'You are fucked' is the punchline, but the SETUP — Paula quoting the exact anodyne corporate compliment — is what makes it land so hard. It's also a joke about workplace terror and performative niceness that lands as true. Quotability is very high: 'Ooh, girl, you are fucked' is a perfect line. Earns its 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: And screw you, you glorified 10%-taking butt boy.

jokes.text: Okay, what he said was: 'I really appreciate the effort you put into your job each day.' Ooh, girl, you are fucked.
jokes.setup: Paula recounts that Larry said something ominous; Darlene asks what he actually said.
jokes.punchline: The quote — totally anodyne corporate praise — is immediately decoded as a death sentence, and Darlene drops the f-word she refused to say moments ago. Double payoff: the meaning of the phrase AND Darlene's hypocrisy.
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke up to this point. It earns a high score because it's a genuine double callback — it pays off Larry's hollow praise AND Darlene's squeamishness about the word 'fucked' in a single line. The structure is near-perfect: the setup (recounting praise) misdirects toward relief, then the punchline flips both expectations simultaneously. 'Ooh, girl, you are fucked' is immediately quotable and delivers on everything the scene built. This is exactly what excellent sitcom construction looks like.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: But it's in the shape of a hat?

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: No, really, Larry, it's kind of embarrassing, because even the arsenio people gave out bathrobes with his big ol' triangle-shaped head on the back.

jokes.text: Artie tries to find the word for Paula's personality flaw: 'abrasive?' 'brusque?' before arriving at 'incapable of putting a performer at ease because she has a basic contempt for the business.'
jokes.setup: Artie is describing what's wrong with Paula to someone (likely on the phone or to another staffer).
jokes.punchline: After rejecting perfectly accurate single-word descriptors, he lands on a dissertation-length diagnosis that is both more specific and more devastating.
jokes.explanation: Rip Torn's Artie rejecting 'abrasive' and 'brusque' as insufficiently precise, then landing on a full psychological indictment, is a great character beat. The escalation from single-word to multi-clause is the structural engine.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: even the arsenio people gave out bathrobes with his big ol' triangle-shaped head on the back

jokes.text: And screw you, you glorified 10%-taking butt boy.
jokes.setup: Paula has been professionally rebuffed by DeVito's agent on the phone.
jokes.punchline: After hanging up (or after being told she can't reach DeVito at home), she unloads on the agent with a tirade that ends in 'glorified 10%-taking butt boy.'
jokes.explanation: 'Butt boy' is a surprising, specific insult that captures Paula's volcanic frustration and her contempt for agents. The 'glorified 10%-taking' qualifier layers in industry specificity. High quotability — feels like something a bitter TV booker would actually say.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Damn it, if this stage caves in, you won't need bathrobes. You'll need bodybags.

jokes.text: Paula, again, no personal calls at work.
jokes.setup: Paula has just unleashed a profane tirade at an agent — clearly a business call.
jokes.punchline: Larry categorizes it as a 'personal call' — either because of the profanity or because he wasn't listening — delivered with total calm.
jokes.explanation: The deadpan misreading of the situation is perfectly timed. Larry's obliviousness (or willful ignorance) of what just happened, expressed in a banal workplace note, is a great Larry beat. Economy: maximal — five words do all the work.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, evidently, we already give a bag.

jokes.text: The hat — 'is it adjustable? Is it one-size-fits-all?' / 'It's a piece of crap.' / 'But it's in the shape of a hat?'
jokes.setup: Larry pivots from the crisis of losing a major guest to obsessively interrogating the quality of the show's gift merchandise.
jokes.punchline: Paula confirms it's garbage; Larry's follow-up — 'But it's in the shape of a hat?' — reveals he's not defending the gift's quality, just its basic structural integrity as a hat.
jokes.explanation: 'But it's in the shape of a hat?' is a great line — it's the floor-of-expectations joke. Larry has retreated so far from 'quality gift' that he's now just checking for hat-ness. Pure character comedy, and it seeds the gift subplot beautifully.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Not if I kill myself before 5:30.

jokes.text: Was that an embroidered actual embroidered patch? Or is it an iron-on patch or what? Do you know?
jokes.setup: In the middle of a booking crisis and earthquake discussion, Larry is now fixated on the manufacturing details of Arsenio's robe patch.
jokes.punchline: The level of specificity — embroidered vs. iron-on — while his building may be structurally compromised, is the absurdist pivot.
jokes.explanation: Part of the sustained Larry-obsesses-over-gifts comedy. The iron-on vs. embroidered distinction is good but the joke is becoming familiar by now. Still true to character.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Or is there just my suit floating in space?

jokes.text: Our gifts bite the biggest bag. / OK, so there's a bag, too?
jokes.setup: Paula uses the idiom 'bite the biggest bag' as an emphatic way of saying the gifts are terrible.
jokes.punchline: Larry takes 'bag' literally, thinking it refers to a gift bag they provide — deadpan literalism.
jokes.explanation: Excellent quick joke. The idiom-taken-literally is a classic comedy structure, but the specificity of 'bag' (as in gift bag) in this gift-obsession context makes it particularly tight. 'OK, so there's a bag, too?' is a great Larry line — his mind jumps to inventory, not insult.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Well, you know, those are made to be seen, not to be worn. They're made to hang in your closet so when someone looks in there they say, 'oh, you've been on arsenio.'

jokes.text: Damn it, if this stage caves in, you won't need bathrobes. You'll need bodybags. Well, evidently, we already give a bag.
jokes.setup: Artie desperately tries to redirect everyone's attention to the life-threatening structural damage. He invokes bodybags.
jokes.punchline: Larry's callback to the 'bag' discussion — 'evidently, we already give a bag' — makes the earthquake a footnote to the gift debate.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's strongest moments. Artie's 'bodybags' line is itself darkly funny, but Larry's deadpan callback — connecting bodybags to the gift-bag discussion — is exceptional. It's a two-layer joke: (1) Artie's dark urgency, (2) Larry's total inability to disengage from his trivial fixation. The callback is earned, perfectly timed, and characterizes Larry's self-absorption at its most dangerous. Earns its 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Milk chocolate necktie. He does.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, those are probably meant to be eaten, not worn.

jokes.text: I just want to say again, what a great job you're doing and how much I appreciate it. / I got Danny DeVito back. / You did? / I did. / Larry! Excuse me.
jokes.setup: Larry begins another round of his ominous HR-speak compliments at Paula.
jokes.punchline: Paula cuts him off by announcing she solved the problem — and Larry's response is childlike wonder ('You did?') followed by him immediately running to tell someone else, dismissing Paula mid-sentence.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the firing-signal compliment works structurally, and Larry's instant abandonment of Paula after she saves the day is character-true. Not as punchy as the original 'great job' joke.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Is that suzanne pleshette? Phil, get out!

jokes.text: How did you get DeVito back? / I didn't. / Well, don't you think that's kind of like a problem? / Not if I kill myself before 5:30.
jokes.setup: Artie asks Paula how she got DeVito back. She admits she didn't.
jokes.punchline: Her contingency plan is suicide before the show airs — delivered with flat matter-of-factness.
jokes.explanation: The workplace-despair-as-dark-comedy beat is well-executed. 'Not if I kill myself before 5:30' has a bureaucratic precision (the 5:30 deadline) that makes the absurdity land harder. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Although, you know, I'd feel a little awkward knowing that strangers were putting their lips on my head.

jokes.text: We give the worst gift in the business. You know that? / Do you even see me standing here? Or is there just my suit floating in space?
jokes.setup: Artie is urgently trying to get Larry to address the earthquake danger. Larry is monologuing about gifts.
jokes.punchline: Artie's exasperated 'is there just my suit floating in space?' expresses his invisibility to Larry in the most vivid possible way.
jokes.explanation: Rip Torn's delivery of 'just my suit floating in space' would be the making of this line. The image is vivid and perfectly captures how Larry makes people feel — present but invisible. Strong craft.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: War of the roses is one of Larry's favorite films. Did I mention that?

jokes.text: They're made to hang in your closet so when someone looks in there they say, 'Oh, you've been on Arsenio.'
jokes.setup: Larry says he doesn't like the heavy feel of Arsenio's robe for actual use.
jokes.punchline: The vendor explains the robe isn't for use — it's a status object, a way to signal you've appeared on Arsenio. The joke is about the entire vanity economy of Hollywood gifts.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely sharp observation about Hollywood gift culture and ego — the robe isn't comfort, it's bragging rights. Industry-insider comedy with real satirical bite.

dialogue.speaker: Danny DeVito
dialogue.line: This is getting very sad. Do you have any shame at all?

jokes.text: You could put my face on the back? / Sure. Let me see your profile. / Oh, you got enough on your mind. / Well— Oh! That would make a great robe. In a thirsty terrycloth? Forget about it.
jokes.setup: Larry asks if his face can go on a gift robe. The vendor offers to look at his profile for the artwork.
jokes.punchline: The vendor's enthusiasm ('Forget about it' in approval) and the specificity of 'thirsty terrycloth' turns what should be a vanity red flag into a joyful collaboration between two people who take this completely seriously.
jokes.explanation: The 'thirsty terrycloth' detail is funny in its specificity — the vendor is now a true believer. Larry's vanity being fed by an eager merchant is a good satirical beat.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I'm like a dog that way. I just have a very bad feeling.

jokes.text: What does Leno give, do you know? / Milk chocolate necktie. / He does. Well, those are probably meant to be eaten, not worn.
jokes.setup: Larry asks about Leno's gifts as competitive research.
jokes.punchline: The revelation that Leno gives milk chocolate neckties is absurd enough, but Larry's earnest analysis — 'meant to be eaten, not worn' — applying the same use-vs-display logic from the robe discussion is the callback payoff.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the worn-vs-displayed distinction is elegant. Milk chocolate necktie is a wonderfully absurd specific detail. Larry applying the same consumer analysis to an edible necktie is peak Larry Sanders logic.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: No, that was Hank clearing his throat.

jokes.text: Paula, I can't do the show tonight. That's why I canceled. I'm very busy. / I thought you said you weren't feeling well. / There's that, too.
jokes.setup: Paula tracks down DeVito and he explains he's too busy. She points out his original excuse was illness.
jokes.punchline: 'There's that, too' — DeVito casually adds illness as a bonus reason, acknowledging both lies are now in play simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: 'There's that, too' is a perfect three-word acknowledgment that the original excuse was fake. The nonchalance makes it funnier. DeVito playing a ruder version of himself is good showbiz satire.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Because twice today, he said that I was doing a really good job.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh... I didn't know he said it twice.

jokes.text: Is that Suzanne Pleshette? Phil, get out!
jokes.setup: Paula is on a high-stakes phone call with DeVito; Phil barges in.
jokes.punchline: Paula's moment of distraction — 'Is that Suzanne Pleshette?' — reveals she's in a celebrity-adjacent environment even while conducting desperate business, then she snaps back.
jokes.explanation: Mild texture joke — the Hollywood-normal of celebrity sightings mid-crisis. Functional but not particularly crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: You're digging a mighty deep hole over there.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Good. Then I can jump in after I shoot myself in the head.

jokes.text: War of the Roses is one of Larry's favorite films. Did I mention that?
jokes.setup: Paula is desperately trying to get DeVito to do the show; she reaches for a personal connection.
jokes.punchline: Mentioning Larry's favorite film in the middle of a booking pitch is a pathetic non-sequitur — DeVito starred in it, but the tactic is transparently sycophantic and Paula knows it ('Did I mention that?' reveals she's improvising wildly).
jokes.explanation: The cringe of a desperate booker name-dropping her boss's film tastes as a relationship-builder is painfully real. 'Did I mention that?' is the tell — she's throwing anything at the wall.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Just think of whatever you would ask a potato lady. And that's all there is to it? And put question marks at the end so Larry knows that they're questions.

jokes.text: This is getting very sad. Do you have any shame at all?
jokes.setup: Paula has been pitching DeVito with increasingly desperate tactics.
jokes.punchline: DeVito's commentary on her behavior — calling it 'very sad' and questioning her shame — functions as a voice for the audience's cringe reaction, which itself becomes funny.
jokes.explanation: A functional cringe beat. DeVito as the straight man here is somewhat unusual. The line works but isn't distinctive.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: And put question marks at the end so Larry knows that they're questions.

jokes.text: Listen, you can come in and do the show. It'll take you 20 minutes, 30 minutes tops. / I have another scene to film. I have to shoot a spot for the juvenile diabetes people, and I'm really not feeling well.
jokes.setup: Paula pushes DeVito to just come do the show quickly.
jokes.punchline: DeVito's escalating stack of excuses — another film scene, a charity PSA, and illness — piles up comedically, especially since he already admitted the illness excuse was an afterthought.
jokes.explanation: The juvenile diabetes PSA becomes plot-important later, so this is setup as much as joke. The excuse-stacking is mildly funny.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: He's putting my photo on the inner thigh. Oh, God damn it. Maybe you're right. Maybe it should be the outer thigh.

jokes.text: You made a commitment to us. Does that mean anything to you? / Good-bye. / Mr. DeVito!
jokes.setup: DeVito has said goodbye and is clearly hanging up.
jokes.punchline: Paula's desperate 'Mr. DeVito!' into a dead line — yelling at a disconnected phone — captures the total impotence of a booker whose only weapon is moral appeal.
jokes.explanation: A solid cringe beat — the morality pitch to a celebrity ('does that mean anything to you?') followed by the dead phone is a good industry-satire moment.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I don't want to talk to the fucking potato lady.

jokes.text: So we're back, basically, to the paperweight-digital clock combination, which you could put my face on? / You seem set on having your face on something.
jokes.setup: Gift options have been evaluated and rejected; Larry revisits an earlier contender.
jokes.punchline: The vendor's observation — 'You seem set on having your face on something' — calls out Larry's real motivation: not guest appreciation but self-promotion.
jokes.explanation: The vendor calling out Larry's narcissism is a great character-truth moment. 'You seem set on having your face on something' functions as the episode's thematic statement delivered by the least consequential character — which makes it land harder.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Um, I think it's just tremendous what you're doing here for juvenile diabetes. And I don't know if you know this, but Larry has low-blood sugar.

dialogue.speaker: DeVito
dialogue.line: It's not the same. Is it? It's not the same.

jokes.text: Whoopi Goldberg mug. / That is nice. / Although, you know, I'd feel a little awkward knowing that strangers were putting their lips on my head.
jokes.setup: The vendor shows Larry a celebrity-branded mug as a gift option.
jokes.punchline: Larry projects himself onto the concept — would HE want strangers' lips on HIS head? — which is both narcissistic and weirdly logical.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best character comedy moments. 'Strangers putting their lips on my head' is a wonderfully specific and personal objection to a gift that isn't even about him yet. The joke works on multiple levels: Larry's narcissism (he's already imagining his face on the mug), his personal space anxiety, and the absurd logic of treating a mug image as physical contact. High quotability, strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Are you telling me that you can't walk 200 feet to plug your own movie? It'll be great exposure, and it'll prevent Larry from firing me. Please?

jokes.text: Is Larry thinking about firing me? / No. What makes you think that? / Because twice today, he said I was doing a really good job.
jokes.setup: Hank asks Artie if Larry is going to fire him.
jokes.punchline: Hank has independently decoded the 'doing a great job' firing signal — the same insight Beverly gave Paula earlier — suggesting this is a well-known Larry behavioral tell.
jokes.explanation: The callback deepens the 'great job' joke by showing it's not just Paula's read — Hank has independently recognized the same signal. This makes Larry's management style a running institutional joke. Good structural payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Iook at this. The name of the horse... Larry's valentine. Jockey... Hank Espinoza. The trainer's name is Bill. Bill, just like the guy who writes for us. Phil. No, it's Bill. See...

jokes.text: Oh, I didn't know he said it twice. / Mm-hmm.
jokes.setup: Hank reveals Larry said the ominous compliment twice to him.
jokes.punchline: Artie's understated 'I didn't know he said it twice' — delivered with the gravity of a medical diagnosis — implies twice is significantly worse than once.
jokes.explanation: Artie's reaction implies a calibrated scale of Larry-compliment severity. The pause implied by 'Mm-hmm' is where the real comedy lives — Rip Torn in reaction is as good as Rip Torn speaking.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: The name of the horse... Larry's valentine. Jockey... Hank Espinoza. The trainer's name is Bill.

jokes.text: You got Danny DeVito on board tonight, don't you? / You bet. / Well, you got nothing to worry about, sweetie.
jokes.setup: Artie reassures Hank that Paula is fine because she has DeVito locked in.
jokes.punchline: The audience knows Paula does NOT have DeVito and is lying to Artie's face — so Artie's reassurance is dramatic irony, and Paula's 'you bet' is a magnificent lie.
jokes.explanation: Good dramatic irony beat — the audience knows more than Artie. 'You bet' from Paula while she has no DeVito is a small but effective cringe moment.

dialogue.speaker: Jimmie Walker
dialogue.line: Guy robs a lady in the subway. The cops come to try to stop this guy. The criminal refuses to stop. They shoot the guy in the back. Paralyze the criminal. The criminal sues the transit system for $4.5 million... and he won the case. Now he's suing nike, 'cause he says if he had had better sneakers, he'd been able to run faster, and they never would have caught him.

jokes.text: You're digging a mighty deep hole over there. / Good. Then I can jump in after I shoot myself in the head.
jokes.setup: Artie comments that Paula is making her situation worse.
jokes.punchline: Paula's response — she'll use the hole for her corpse after she shoots herself — is a dark escalation of the 5:30 suicide joke.
jokes.explanation: The callback to self-destruction works and the logistics of the joke (needing both a gun and a hole) are darkly specific. Paula's despair-as-dark-comedy is a consistent and effective character note.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Where is he? He's in make-up.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: One more segment with the potato lady, and then Danny...

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I'm not doing a dumb segment with the potato lady.

jokes.text: I need you to prepare the potato lady interview questions. / I have no idea how to do that. / That has never stopped me before. / Just think of whatever you would ask a potato lady. / And that's all there is to it? / And put question marks at the end so Larry knows that they're questions.
jokes.setup: Paula desperately delegates the interview prep to Beverly, who has zero qualifications.
jokes.punchline: Paula's coaching is: (1) just think of what you'd ask a potato lady, and (2) put question marks at the end. The procedural specificity of 'so Larry knows they're questions' is the absurdist cherry.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely excellent comedy beat. The instruction to 'put question marks at the end so Larry knows they're questions' is the kind of absurdist workplace detail that feels real and ridiculous simultaneously. It implies Larry needs formatting to understand interrogatives, which is both a burn on Larry and an indictment of TV-host prep. High originality, strong structure.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I got to tell you the truth. I'm torn but, uh... madison is who it looks like to me. I would take another guess if I were you.

jokes.text: I ordered the Larry Sanders jogging suits. I think the guests are gonna love 'em. And the guy says he can have them all delivered by tonight.
jokes.setup: The gift debate has been ongoing; Hank appears backstage having taken unilateral action.
jokes.punchline: Hank has ordered jogging suits branded with Larry's face without authorization — completely bypassing the gift committee that has been agonizing over this decision.
jokes.explanation: Hank's executive action on the gift problem — solving it in the most Hank way possible — is a good character beat. The comedy is that he's simultaneously helpful and completely overstepping.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I never had the bad feeling worse than I do right now.

jokes.text: He's putting my photo on the inner thigh. / Oh, God damn it. / Maybe you're right. Maybe it should be the outer thigh.
jokes.setup: Larry reveals where on the jogging suit his photo will be placed.
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'Oh, God damn it' is the reaction; Larry's response to that reaction is to earnestly consider whether the outer thigh would be better — missing the point entirely.
jokes.explanation: Strong joke. 'Inner thigh' is already absurdly intimate for a photo placement. But Larry interpreting Artie's 'God damn it' as a critique of PLACEMENT rather than the concept itself — and responding 'maybe it should be the outer thigh' — is perfectly calibrated Larry Sanders obliviousness. Character integration is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: DeVito
dialogue.line: Late? I just decided 5 minutes ago to do the show. What do you mean late?

jokes.text: Don't talk to me the way I would be talking to me.
jokes.setup: Someone (Beverly or Larry) is being diplomatic and telling Artie what he wants to hear.
jokes.punchline: Artie's self-aware instruction not to handle him with the same BS he himself uses — 'the way I would be talking to me' — is a flash of Artie's self-knowledge.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best line. 'Don't talk to me the way I would be talking to me' is exceptional — it's a single sentence that reveals Artie's complete self-awareness about his own management BS, his intelligence, and his frustration. The syntax is perfectly twisted: hearing himself being managed the way he manages others is nauseating to him. Economy is maximum — nine words that do the work of a monologue. Quotability is among the highest in the episode. Earns its 8+ score comfortably.

dialogue.speaker: DeVito
dialogue.line: Well, your booker, she said that you were going to fire her if... if I didn't, uh, show up. I don't want that on my conscious. She's troubled.

jokes.text: Is he on something? / No, just the same 2 things, except I think he took them together today. / Well, he had the pepperoni pizza for lunch, that should soak it up.
jokes.setup: Artie is behaving erratically; a staffer is asked if something is wrong with him.
jokes.punchline: The casual confirmation that Artie takes two substances, occasionally together, followed by the equally casual pharmaceutical remedy of 'pepperoni pizza should soak it up' — treating substance management as a normal workplace logistics problem.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the normalization — Artie's drug use is not a crisis but a scheduling item, and pizza is the fix. 'That should soak it up' delivered straight is what makes this land. Great character comedy about the chaotic backstage of TV production.

dialogue.speaker: Danny DeVito
dialogue.line: your booker, she said that you were going to fire her if... if I didn't, uh, show up. I don't want that on my conscious.

jokes.text: These potato lady questions are terrible. / Well, what would you ask the potato lady? / That's Paula's job. I don't want to talk to the f***ing potato lady.
jokes.setup: Larry is upset about the interview prep Beverly/Hank did for the potato lady segment.
jokes.punchline: Larry's definitive 'I don't want to talk to the fucking potato lady' — the clearest possible statement of his feelings about this novelty segment he's agreed to do.
jokes.explanation: The explicitness of 'I don't want to talk to the fucking potato lady' is funny because it's the undisguised truth behind the late-night host's professional obligations. Every host has a potato lady; Larry just says so.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Now I look like one of those pussies who got under the desk.

jokes.text: Hello. I'm Danny DeVito. You know, juvenile diabetes affects over 120 children in this country... uh, oh. All right. OK. I'm sorry. 120,000 children in this country...
jokes.setup: DeVito is shooting a PSA for juvenile diabetes — his stated excuse for not doing the talk show.
jokes.punchline: He immediately blows the most basic fact of the PSA — 120 vs. 120,000 children — making his 'too important to do a talk show' excuse look absurd.
jokes.explanation: The payoff on DeVito's 'I'm doing something important' excuse is that he can't even execute the PSA correctly. The scale error (120 vs. 120,000) is a specific and well-calibrated error — not zero, not wildly wrong, just a factor of 1,000 off.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Hot to trot. OK, I knew it. Breathe.

jokes.text: I think it's just tremendous what you're doing here for juvenile diabetes. And I don't know if you know this, but Larry has low-blood sugar. / It's not the same. / Is it?
jokes.setup: Paula has crashed the PSA shoot and is trying to bond with DeVito over diabetes.
jokes.punchline: She claims Larry's low blood sugar as a diabetes connection. DeVito corrects her ('it's not the same'). Paula's genuinely uncertain 'Is it?' reveals she doesn't know the difference but was willing to weaponize Larry's snack schedule.
jokes.explanation: Excellent cringe comedy. The weaponization of Larry's blood sugar as a diabetes connection is both pathetic and brilliant. 'Is it?' — her genuine uncertainty — is what elevates it from a standard bad-pitch joke to something special. She truly wasn't sure.

dialogue.speaker: DeVito
dialogue.line: if I'm gonna die, I want to die with my family, not with jimmie walker and the weirdo with the doughnuts. Potatoes? The potato lady? Whatever.

jokes.text: Are you telling me that you can't walk 200 feet to plug your own movie? It'll be great exposure, and it'll prevent Larry from firing me. Please?
jokes.setup: DeVito keeps refusing. Paula has run out of professional arguments.
jokes.punchline: She abandons all pretense and makes the ask purely personal — 'it'll prevent Larry from firing me' — as the actual argument. The 'please?' is devastating.
jokes.explanation: The nakedness of the ask is the joke — she's dropped the professional framing entirely and is begging for her job. '200 feet to plug your own movie' is also a great line because it makes DeVito's refusal seem absurd from a self-interest perspective. 'Please?' as the closing argument is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: the jogging suit is just a wrapping, sir, inside, you'll find a lovely silver desk clock from tiffany.

dialogue.speaker: DeVito
dialogue.line: Silverplate?

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Solid silver, Mr. D. Swiss movement.

jokes.text: Bill Clinton. Very topical. / Yeah, for a couple more years.
jokes.setup: A writer pitches a Clinton joke as timely.
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'for a couple more years' — acknowledging the shelf life of presidential jokes — is a dry, insider observation about late-night topicality.
jokes.explanation: A quick, efficient meta-joke about the nature of topical comedy. Works on its own terms; nothing special structurally.

dialogue.speaker: Danny DeVito
dialogue.line: Potatoes? The potato lady? Whatever.

jokes.text: Listen, I think I got something live in the fifth at Santa Anita tomorrow. / The name of the horse: Larry's Valentine. / Jockey: Hank Espinoza. / The trainer's name is Bill. / Phil. / No, it's Bill. See... / Phil is the name of the guy who writes for us. / Listen, you want to get in on this or don't you?
jokes.setup: Hank pitches Larry a horse racing tip based on an elaborate string of coincidences involving the horse's name, jockey, and trainer.
jokes.punchline: The jockey is 'Hank Espinoza' (Hank's delight in his own name appearing), the trainer is 'Bill' — but the writer is Phil, not Bill — and Hank refuses to let the factual error undermine his certainty, dismissing the correction entirely.
jokes.explanation: Classic Hank — his pattern-matching superstition leads to a tip whose logic collapses the moment it's examined, but he's committed regardless. 'Listen, you want to get in on this or don't you?' is a perfect Hank line: impatient with scrutiny.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Oh, hell, yes. We could put your cock on it. As long as it's not the hour hand.

jokes.text: Oh, you know him. He's always late. / He is not always late. He's usually here a couple hours ahead of time just to tell me how much he hates doing talk shows and how uncomfortable he is. He'll be here.
jokes.setup: Larry asks about DeVito's status. Artie or a staffer says 'oh, you know him, he's always late.'
jokes.punchline: Larry corrects this — DeVito arrives early, but only to complain about being there. His early arrival is worse than lateness.
jokes.explanation: Sharp Hollywood satire about the particular performer type who shows up early to preemptively hate the experience. The inversion — early arrival as worse behavior — is a good structural turn.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: You wouldn't believe that lengths I have to go to. The other week, when Tom hanks tried to back out, I had to cry and feign illness.

jokes.text: Jimmie Walker's prepared to stretch. / Crime is terrible. I don't have to tell you guys...
jokes.setup: If DeVito doesn't show, Jimmie Walker can fill time.
jokes.punchline: Cut to Walker already on stage doing his act — a broad, low-energy crime observations bit that immediately confirms 'stretching with Jimmie Walker' is a desperate fallback.
jokes.explanation: The cut TO Walker mid-routine — and the routine being exactly what you'd expect from a faded '70s comedian filling time — is meta-commentary on late-night desperation. The joke is the juxtaposition of the crisis backstage and the dead-earnest material onstage.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: muffin mania gifts. It's endless.

jokes.text: Jimmie Walker's crime joke: criminal sues Nike because he'd have run faster in better sneakers, and won.
jokes.setup: Walker is doing a crime bit about a criminal who was shot and paralyzed by police.
jokes.punchline: The criminal sues Nike, arguing better sneakers would have allowed him to escape — and won the case.
jokes.explanation: The Walker material is intentionally mediocre — that's the joke (see Joke 50). Taken on its own terms, the Nike lawsuit punchline is functional mid-tier stand-up: absurdist legal logic, mildly clever, but not sharp. The show is using Walker's actual material to characterize the desperation of the booking situation.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Bob uecker, Shari Lewis, and the seashell man. And sting.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Oh, have we got sting? You betcha. Great.

jokes.text: Is Danny DeVito really on his way? / I have no idea. They kicked me off the set.
jokes.setup: Larry asks for a status update on DeVito during the show.
jokes.punchline: Paula's admission — 'I have no idea. They kicked me off the set' — reveals she crashed a PSA shoot and was physically removed, now reporting from total uncertainty.
jokes.explanation: 'They kicked me off the set' is a great line — the matter-of-fact reporting of her own ejection. It implies a whole chaotic scene and delivers it in six words.

jokes.text: I could call David Copperfield and ask him to do the show. He owes me one. / I'll bet he does.
jokes.setup: Larry floats calling in a favor from David Copperfield as a DeVito replacement.
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'I'll bet he does' — delivered without elaboration — implies the nature of the favor is something Artie doesn't want to know about, or something Artie definitely knows about.
jokes.explanation: 'I'll bet he does' does a lot with four words — it implies a whole story about what Larry did for/to David Copperfield. The comedy is entirely in what's NOT said. Economy score is near-maximum.

jokes.text: What is it? / Thomas Jefferson. / This is a very exciting development.
jokes.setup: The potato lady shows Larry a potato that resembles something.
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'this is a very exciting development' — delivered in full late-night host sincerity — is the perfect expression of a man who has to treat a Thomas Jefferson potato as breaking news.
jokes.explanation: Larry's professional enthusiasm for the absolutely banal is a perfect character beat. 'This is a very exciting development' for a potato shaped like Jefferson is Larry at his most performatively engaged.

jokes.text: Have you ever eaten a raw potato? / You don't... well, you know, I have such a personal relationship with them that...
jokes.setup: Someone asks the potato lady about eating raw potatoes.
jokes.punchline: Her hesitation and 'personal relationship' framing implies eating a potato would be like cannibalism from her perspective — she can't answer because the question is fundamentally disturbing to her.
jokes.explanation: The potato lady's 'personal relationship' with potatoes implies an emotional bond that makes eating one unthinkable — a quietly absurdist character detail that rewards the absurdity of the segment.

jokes.text: What were you thinking about with these potato questions? / I got to go. / What were you thinking of? / You know, Artie, I did eat a raw potato once, and the taste was quite unusual. I thought it was a good question.
jokes.setup: Artie confronts Beverly about the terrible interview questions she wrote.
jokes.punchline: Beverly defends herself by revealing she drew on personal experience — she ate a raw potato once — as her research methodology. Her pride in the question is unshakeable.
jokes.explanation: Beverly's earnest defense of her raw potato research is good character comedy. The confidence with which she stands behind her question is the joke — she is satisfied with her work.

jokes.text: I never had the bad feeling worse than I do right now. / I'm torn, but... Madison is who it looks like to me. / I would take another guess if I were you.
jokes.setup: Artie has a premonition of disaster (earthquake); the potato lady is showing her potatoes to Hank for identification.
jokes.punchline: Hank guesses 'Madison' for a presidential potato — wrong — while Artie is having a crisis of premonition. The juxtaposition of Artie's dread and Hank's potato-guessing is absurdist comedy by contrast.
jokes.explanation: The tonal juxtaposition is the joke — Artie's genuine foreboding runs alongside Hank earnestly guessing potato presidents. Good use of parallel action for comedy.

jokes.text: Where's Danny? / You were so great with the potato lady. / Where is he?
jokes.setup: Larry urgently asks where DeVito is. A staffer deflects with a compliment about the potato lady segment.
jokes.punchline: Larry ignores the transparent deflection and repeats his question — the non-answer is so obvious Larry doesn't even process it as a compliment.
jokes.explanation: A functional scene beat — the transparently sycophantic deflection is recognizable. Not particularly crafted but serves the pacing.

jokes.text: I just decided 5 minutes ago to do the show. What do you mean late?
jokes.setup: Larry gently chides DeVito for being late.
jokes.punchline: DeVito is baffled — he only decided to come 5 minutes ago, so he can't be late relative to his own decision timeline. His logic is airtight from his perspective.
jokes.explanation: DeVito's logic is genuinely funny — he's not wrong from inside his own worldview. The solipsism of the celebrity: reality conforms to when he decided to participate, not to external schedules.

jokes.text: Well, your booker — she said that you were going to fire her if I didn't show up. I don't want that on my conscious. / She's troubled.
jokes.setup: DeVito explains why he actually came — Paula's confession.
jokes.punchline: Larry's instant diagnosis: 'She's troubled.' Not apologetic, not embarrassed — clinical. The speed of the pivot is the joke.
jokes.explanation: 'She's troubled' is a great Larry line — it's simultaneously dismissive, self-protective, and funny because it reframes his own threatening behavior as her psychological problem. Economy is near-perfect. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Did you tell Danny DeVito that I was going to fire you if he didn't do the show? / I didn't use those exact words. / Well, do you realize what inappropriate behavior that is? / Do you realize how badly that reflects on me? / Am I fired now?
jokes.setup: Larry confronts Paula about her confession to DeVito.
jokes.punchline: Paula's 'Am I fired now?' — cutting through Larry's moral lecture to the only question that matters — is a perfect deflation of his indignation. She's not contrite; she's just checking her employment status.
jokes.explanation: Paula cutting Larry's lecture with a direct employment status question is a great character beat. She's not apologizing — she's auditing the situation.

jokes.text: Was that an aftershock? / I believe it was. / OK, well — we live in Southern California, we dress in Southern California, and we do a show in Southern California.
jokes.setup: An actual aftershock hits during the live show, interrupting Larry's introduction of DeVito.
jokes.punchline: Larry's ad-lib response — 'we live in Southern California, we dress in Southern California, and we do a show in Southern California' — is a perfect piece of professional patter that means absolutely nothing but sounds calming.
jokes.explanation: The triple parallel structure ('we live... we dress... we do a show') applied to a crisis situation is a beautiful piece of late-night host improv comedy — it sounds substantive but says nothing. Character integration is high: only Larry Sanders would respond to an earthquake this way.

jokes.text: Hank, sit down. / Let's not overreact... / OK! / That would be... another one? / Why don't we take a break and let Hank collect himself?
jokes.setup: The first aftershock hits; Hank panics visibly on camera. A second shock follows.
jokes.punchline: Larry, trying to project calm, ultimately has to offer Hank a break to 'collect himself' — the euphemism for 'you just had a meltdown on live television' is perfectly understated.
jokes.explanation: Hank's on-air panic is perfect Tambor physical comedy, and 'let Hank collect himself' is a masterclass in Larry's professional face-saving instinct. The escalation of two shocks, each worse than the last for Hank's composure, is well-structured.

jokes.text: Now I look like one of those pussies who got under the desk.
jokes.setup: The cameras are off. Hank has just visibly panicked on live TV.
jokes.punchline: His complaint is not that he panicked, but that he's been visually associated with desk-duckers — the image problem, not the terror, is his concern.
jokes.explanation: Peak Hank: his vanity survives his terror. The fact that his concern after an earthquake is his on-camera image — specifically being grouped with 'pussies who got under the desk' — is a perfect character revelation. Strong economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Welcome to Shakeytown. Enjoy the music.
jokes.setup: Post-aftershock chaos. Larry and the crew are rattled.
jokes.punchline: Artie's sardonic 'Welcome to Shakeytown. Enjoy the music' — a tour-guide delivery for a potentially deadly situation — is his characteristic dark wit.
jokes.explanation: 'Welcome to Shakeytown. Enjoy the music.' is a highly quotable Artie line — the deadpan hospitality framing for a structural disaster is perfectly in character for Rip Torn's Artie. Economy is near-perfect. Two sentences do everything.

jokes.text: Now I want you to breathe. Come on — do that. Good. Now, when you're doing that, do you have any good or bad feelings about any of these names... Daddy's Girl... breathe... Lucky Lindy, Hot to Trot... any feelings at all? / Hot to Trot. / Good. I knew it.
jokes.setup: Artie is trying to calm Larry down post-earthquake while simultaneously mining him for horse-racing tips (using Larry's earthquake 'bad feeling' as a psychic instrument).
jokes.punchline: Artie calmly walks Larry through the horse names while coaching his breathing — the therapeutic framing is entirely in service of gambling research.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's two or three best jokes. Artie's therapeutic manner — 'breathe... breathe' — is entirely weaponized for extracting horse-race intuitions from a panicking Larry. The comedy is in the total moral clarity of Artie's priorities: earthquake = opportunity to harvest Larry's psychic feelings about horses. Character integration is exceptional — this scene could only exist in this show with these characters. The callback to Hank's horse tip and Artie's own 'bad feeling' premonitions is elegant. Earns its 8+ score.

jokes.text: Stage 2, Stage 9, or Stage 12? / 2. Let's go to Stage 2. / Or 9. 2 or 9. I don't know. / I can't make a decision, but we gotta get out of here.
jokes.setup: Artie finally gets Larry to address the stage decision — the urgent safety matter he's been avoiding all episode.
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately proves he can't make decisions — he cycles through options without landing — while insisting they must leave immediately. Urgency + indecision = chaos.
jokes.explanation: Larry's decision-making paralysis under pressure is a good character beat — the man who spent the episode obsessing over gift details can't decide between three numbered stages. Good payoff on his earlier evasions.

jokes.text: Look, I'm out of here. I appreciate you inviting me down to do the show, but I'm going. / Wait a minute. We haven't even done your segment yet. You're next. / If I'm gonna die, I want to die with my family, not with Jimmie Walker and the weirdo with the doughnuts. / Potatoes? The potato lady? / Whatever.
jokes.setup: Post-earthquake, DeVito announces he's leaving before his segment.
jokes.punchline: His explanation — he'd rather die with family than with 'Jimmie Walker and the weirdo with the doughnuts' — reduces the potato lady to 'weirdo with doughnuts,' and his 'whatever' when corrected is perfect celebrity dismissal.
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. 'The weirdo with the doughnuts' is a great misremembering, and the 'whatever' when corrected captures celebrity indifference perfectly. 'If I'm gonna die, I want to die with my family, not with Jimmie Walker' is also a quietly devastating line about the social hierarchy of a TV green room.

jokes.text: We've got a beautiful gift for you. / I already got a Larry Sanders t-shirt. / But this is a Larry Sanders jogging suit. / I got plenty of jogging suits. Not like this. This is a multi-colored... / The jogging suit is just a wrapping, sir. Inside you'll find a lovely silver desk clock from Tiffany.
jokes.setup: DeVito is leaving; Larry/Artie deploys the new gift to keep him.
jokes.punchline: The Tiffany clock reveal — the jogging suit was just packaging — is the episode's gift-subplot climax. DeVito stops for a Tiffany clock.
jokes.explanation: Strong structural payoff on the gift debate — the Tiffany clock (wrapped in a Larry Sanders jogging suit) is what finally gets DeVito to stay. The gift subplot, which seemed like Larry's obsessive tangent, turns out to actually solve the episode's crisis. Good comedic architecture.

jokes.text: Silverplate? / Solid silver, Mr. D. / Swiss movement. / All right, I'll see you out there.
jokes.setup: DeVito, being wooed by the clock offer, checks its quality.
jokes.punchline: He demands to know if it's solid silver (not plate) and Swiss movement — and these are his breaking points. He's entirely won over by luxury specifications.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of DeVito's due diligence — he won't commit until he knows it's solid silver and Swiss — is a great celebrity-vanity beat. 'All right, I'll see you out there' after satisfactory answers is perfectly timed.

jokes.text: They can put my face on those, right? / Oh, hell, yes. We could put your cock on it. / As long as it's not the hour hand.
jokes.setup: Larry, relieved, asks about the branding on the clocks.
jokes.punchline: Artie escalates to 'we could put your cock on it,' and Larry's comeback — 'as long as it's not the hour hand' — is a self-deprecating dirty joke.
jokes.explanation: Larry's 'as long as it's not the hour hand' is the best dirty joke in the episode — it's self-deprecating (implying he's not well-endowed) and perfectly timed after Artie's escalation. It's a rare moment of Larry being genuinely funny rather than anxious. High quotability.

jokes.text: Eddie, go up to my office. Bring down that clock on my desk, will you? The silver one. You know, the one that Larry gave me for Christmas last year.
jokes.setup: Artie has promised DeVito a silver Tiffany clock. He now needs to source one immediately.
jokes.punchline: He's regifting Larry's Christmas gift to him — giving it to DeVito to get him on the show. He's stripping Larry's gift from his own office to solve Larry's booking problem.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely great comedy beat that also works as a perfect structural payoff. Artie is regifting Larry's own Christmas present to get a guest on Larry's show — the circularity is elegant. It also says everything about Artie's pragmatism and Larry's obliviousness. Strong character integration — this is an Artie solution.

jokes.text: I want to say that I think the segment with Danny DeVito went really, really well, and I think that you were extremely hilarious with the potato lady. / Yeah, well, I think we all know that.
jokes.setup: Paula opens her post-show conversation with Larry with excessive praise — trying to soften the firing conversation.
jokes.punchline: Larry accepts the compliment completely without irony — 'yeah, well, I think we all know that' — not noticing it's flattery, just agreeing.
jokes.explanation: Larry's unironic self-agreement is a good character beat — he can't detect flattery because he genuinely believes himself. The 'we all know that' is a nice, small character moment.

jokes.text: I gotta say that about 3 times a week to get guests to do this show. / You do? / You wouldn't believe the lengths I have to go to. The other week, when Tom Hanks tried to back out, I had to cry and feign illness. I mean, muffin mania gifts. It's endless.
jokes.setup: Paula defends her DeVito manipulation by revealing it's standard operating procedure.
jokes.punchline: The revelation that Paula cries, feigns illness, and bribes with 'muffin mania gifts' weekly to book guests — and that Tom Hanks is no easier than DeVito — is a sharp indictment of late-night booking.
jokes.explanation: Paula's industry confessional is sharp — 'muffin mania gifts' as a booking tool is a wonderful specific detail, and the Tom Hanks example shows the problem isn't DeVito-specific. Strong character comedy with real industry-satire backbone.

jokes.text: Who do you have on tap for tomorrow night? / Bob Uecker, Shari Lewis, and the seashell man. / And sting. / Oh, have we got sting? / You betcha.
jokes.setup: Episode closing: Larry asks for tomorrow's lineup, echoing the opening scene structure.
jokes.punchline: The lineup — Bob Uecker, Shari Lewis, the seashell man — is another collection of nobodies and novelty acts at the same level as today's potato lady. Then 'and Sting' is buried at the end like an afterthought, making the same joke as the DeVito/Jimmie Walker juxtaposition.
jokes.explanation: The closing callback to the opening lineup structure is a formally elegant button. 'The seashell man' as the potato lady's successor is perfect, and burying Sting at the end — making a rock legend an afterthought after the seashell man — is a structurally sound closer. Good episode architecture.

tmdb_overview: Paula worries about her job when Larry gets angry with her over guests canceling, and really goes all out to convince a reluctant Danny DeVito not to cancel too. Larry and Artie try to decide what to choose as the guest gift.
